 City Hall tackles El Niño, traffic, data centers, and ‘sober spaces’  
 Emergency planning, surveillance, and traffic safety are hot topics this week. Plus legislation hotels are none too pleased about, and a plan to buoy Mid-Market with lawyers 
 by 
 Mike Ege 
 November 15, 2026 November 16, 2026 
 Share this:
 Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)

 X 
 From a deck by contractor AECOM: want to save businesses? Easy– corral lawyers. | Courtesy AECOM and SF Board of Supervisors 
 San Francisco lawmakers will have a busy, varied agenda this week as they consider legislation on issues ranging from hotel workers’ ability to sue their employers over health issues to restrictions on data centers, along with hearings on traffic safety and revitalizing Market Street. Meanwhile, commissions review surveillance policy and the state of cleanup at the former Hunters Point shipyard. 
 El Niño, data centers, and traffic safety 
 One of the first events on this week’s calendar is a Monday meeting of the city’s Disaster Council , chaired by Mayor Daniel Lurie and Department of Emergency Management Executive Director Mary Ellen Carroll , to review preparations for anticipated extreme weather events associated with El Niño .
 The meeting comes as officials consider the potential for heavier rainfall, flooding, and other weather-related disruptions from the climate pattern, and Lurie’s declaration of a city emergency last month, to expedite department response. The council includes the heads of the Police and Fire departments, Public Health, Public Works, the Port, the Municipal Transportation Agency and other city departments.
 A presentation for the meeting obtained by The Voice outlines the roles of different departments to coordinate preparedness, protect the city’s waterfront, drainage systems, transport, and public spaces from flooding, and generally “mitigate what we can and prepare to respond to impacts we cannot prevent.” 
 Later that day, the Supervisors’ Land Use Committee considers items related to the interim moratorium on data centers, including a move to extend the freeze for another 10 months. The debate comes amid growing scrutiny of the potential environmental and land-use consequences of data centers, including their substantial electricity and water requirements.
 The committee will likely refer the extension and other items to the full board for approval on Tuesday; as an extension of emergency legislation, it will require nine votes for passage. 
 The committee will also reopen a hearing convened by Board President Rafael Mandelman , along with colleagues Stephen Sherrill and Danny Sauter , on traffic enforcement and street safety. The hearing was originally convened in 2022, when it revealed significant deficits in enforcement, including a 97 percent decline in citations between 2014 and 2022, with less than half issued for the five violations most commonly associated with serious collisions.  Subsequent meetings have found little improvement, and a 2025 Civil Grand Jury report found that police failed to prioritize traffic safety and had inadequate staffing. 
 Health Commission reviews Hunters Point cleanup 
 Also on Monday, the Health Commission will hear a presentation from the Department of Public Health on the Hunters Point Naval Shipyard . The presentation , by Health Officer Susan Philip and other department officials, will cover remediation and restoration updates, health promotion in Bayview-Hunters Point, community outreach and regulatory oversight.
 The presentation includes updates on the July 2026 vegetation fire at the shipyard’s Parcel E-2 landfill, which burned an estimated two to three acres and damaged monitoring equipment and stormwater controls. The Navy subsequently repaired the damaged systems, while state regulators and the Health Department monitored the response.
 Full board: Strengthening the Healthy Buildings Ordinance 
 Set for approval on first reading at Tuesday’s Board of Supervisors meeting is a Covid-era ordinance requiring hotels to follow specified cleaning and disease-prevention practices, including frequent cleaning of high-contact common areas. A proposed amendment would allow hotel employees and their unions to sue hotels for civil penalties and other remedies. The bill is sponsored by District 11 Supervisor Chyanne Chen , with Mandelman and colleagues Connie Chan, Shamann Walton and Jackie Fielder as cosponsors. After being held on ice at the Rules Committee since April, it was revived with amendments earlier this month.
 In a Nov. 14 oped in the Chronicle , Lynn S. Mohrfeld , president and CEO of the California Hotel and Lodging Association , criticized the proposal as expanding outdated pandemic-era requirements. The group has also placed ads on social media to coincide with the vote. 
 Budget Committee: Can relocating courts jumpstart Mid-Market?
 On Wednesday, the supervisors’ Budget and Finance Committee will consider a bill sponsored by District 6 member Matt Dorsey and almost all his colleagues to enable “Sober Spaces” by increasing availability of public facilities such as community rooms to recovery groups at no cost, along with a fund to support such meetings when hosted by private nonprofit-owned facilities. 
 Dorsey will also preside over a hearing on how to use city-owned assets to help revitalize Market Street. One presentation associated with the hearing explores the leveraging of courthouses for economic impact, and Dorsey has floated the idea of moving the Hall of Justice and related offices to the struggling Mid- Market area. 
 Police Commission: Surveillance cameras 
 Meanwhile the Police Commission will hear a briefing on on its live monitoring of surveillance cameras owned by private entities and other non-city organizations. Current city laws allow officers to access private camera feeds in emergencies involving imminent danger, certain significant public-safety events and active criminal investigations, with restrictions. They were enacted after a controversy in 2020 over the practice during the George Floyd protests. 
 The department’s presentation reports that all requests for live monitoring from the third quarter of 2023 through the first half of 2026 were approved. During the first six months of this year, SFPD made 11 requests, involving 40 hours and 58 minutes of monitoring, and reported 10 arrests.
 Oversight Committee: Mission chaos and schools 
 Finally, on Thursday, the Supervisors’ Government Audit and Oversight Committee will hold a hearing, called for by Fielder, on street conditions adjacent to public schools. 
 The hearing will examine reports of human waste, discarded needles, accumulated garbage and unauthorized encampments near school entrances, and the city’s response to those conditions. The committee has requested reports from the Mayor’s Office, San Francisco Unified School District, Public Works, the Department of Public Health’s Street Needs Team and emergency services officials.
 The hearing will likely put much of its focus on Marshall Elementary School in her district, which the Chronicle has described as “Ground Zero for chaos in the Mission,” in the Mission District, where students and staff have faced daily exposure to public drug use, human waste, needles, and violence.
